title: Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries
claim: Existing objectives predict only the next token or a few discrete future tokens; ours predict a compact summary of the whole future.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid, token rows with dashed arrows to targets
description: A 2x2 grid of token-sequence diagrams comparing four training objectives. Each panel has a bold label (NTP, MTP, FSP-BoW, FSP-RevLM). In each, a large green block labeled x_{≤t} (the prefix) is followed by a row of orange token boxes x_{t+1}, x_{t+2}, ..., x_{T-1}, x_T. Dashed arrows run from the prefix to its prediction targets. NTP highlights only x_{t+1}, with the later tokens greyed out and a dashed arrow to an empty-set symbol. MTP highlights several future tokens, each with its own arrow. The FSP panels have all future tokens in orange. In FSP-BoW, solid arrows feed those tokens into a grey box labeled 'Bag-of-words (multi-hot vector)', which a dashed arrow from the prefix targets. In FSP-RevLM the grey box reads 'Hidden Representation of Reverse LM'. The eye goes first to the green prefix blocks, then to the grey summary boxes in the bottom row.
caption: A comparison of future-aware pretraining objectives. All methods take a prefix $x_{\leq t}$ as input. NTP: Only predicts the immediate next token. MTP: Uses multiple auxiliary heads, each predicting a specific future token. FSP-BoW: Our proposed hand-crafted summary method that predicts a multi-hot "bag-of-tokens" summary of a long future window using a single auxiliary head. FSP-RevLM: Our proposed learned summary method predicts a compact hidden representation of the future, which is generated by a reverse language model (RevLM).
abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) has driven the success of large language models (LLMs), but it struggles with long-horizon reasoning, planning, and creative writing, with these limitations largely attributed to teacher-forced training. Multi-token prediction (MTP) partially mitigates these issues by predicting several future tokens at once, but it mostly captures short-range dependencies and offers limited improvement. We propose future summary prediction (FSP), which trains an auxiliary head to predict a compact representation of the long-term future, preserving information relevant for long-form generations. We explore two variants of FSP: handcrafted summaries, for example, a bag of words summary of the future sequence, and learned summaries, which use embeddings produced by a reverse language model trained from right-to-left order. Large-scale pretraining experiments (3B and 8B-parameter models) demonstrate that FSP provides improvements over both NTP and MTP across math, reasoning, and coding benchmarks.
